q: Which space planning principle means spaces adapt to users' changing needs?
n: Flexibility means spaces can be reconfigured or adapted as users' needs change over time. Source: Karlen, Space Planning Basics; Time-Saver Standards for Interior Design.

q: What is a principle of good space planning that tailors spaces to different functions?
n: Flexibility in space planning lets a space be tailored to serve different functions. Source: Karlen, Space Planning Basics.

q: What is a principle of good space planning where spaces have logical access?
n: Efficiency means every space has logical, direct access, with minimal wasted circulation and sensible adjacencies. Source: Karlen, Space Planning Basics.

q: Which is NOT a space planning concern?
n: Function, users and circulation are space-planning concerns. Topography is a site-planning concern. Source: Karlen, Space Planning Basics; Lynch & Hack, Site Planning.

q: Which statement is NOT part of space planning?
o: How the building's character fits the community
How people spend their time inside
n: How the building's character fits the community is an urban design or architectural concern. Space planning deals with movement, users and activities inside. Source: Karlen, Space Planning Basics.

q: Which of these is NOT a space planning consideration?
n: Selecting engineering consultants is a project-management task. Privacy, lighting and ventilation, and accessibility are space-planning considerations. Source: Karlen, Space Planning Basics; UAP SPP Doc. 202.

q: What is the key factor in designing functional spaces?
n: Functional space design starts from user needs and preferences. Cost, materials and aesthetics follow from what users must do in the space. Source: Karlen, Space Planning Basics; Panero & Zelnik, Human Dimension & Interior Space.

q: Which principle stresses ease of movement?
n: Efficient circulation is the principle of easy, logical movement between spaces. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space & Order; Karlen.

q: Which is NOT one of Ching's forms of spatial organization?
n: Ching's spatial organizations are centralized, linear, radial, clustered and grid. "Vertical" is not one of them. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space & Order.

q: What paved outdoor space next to a house is used for dining?
n: A patio is a paved outdoor area next to a house, used for dining and leisure. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: In space planning which statement below is NOT relevant?
o: Space planning is a process that takes several steps and is an important component for the works of architects.
Space planning helps ensure efficient use of floor space without wasting
Space planning is an in-depth analysis of how physical space is used in a structure
Space planning is the efficient use of floor space of utilities
n: Space planning is a multi-step process for arranging interior spaces around users and activities. Describing it as using floor space for utilities misstates it, so that statement is not relevant. Source: Karlen, Space Planning Basics.

q: Space planning starts by gathering information such as:
n: Space planning starts by establishing the purpose of each space through programming. The development plan, lot description and zoning are site and planning data. Source: Karlen, Space Planning Basics.

q: What is the desirable width range, in meters, of a restaurant service aisle (Time-Saver Standards)?
n: Time-Saver Standards gives about 1.20–1.50 m as the desirable width of a restaurant service aisle, enough for servers with trays to pass seated guests. Source: Time-Saver Standards for Building Types (Restaurants).

q: What is the desirable clearance, in meters, between a wall and a restaurant seat back (Time-Saver Standards upper value)?
n: Time-Saver Standards gives a wall-to-seat-back clearance of up to about 0.76 m (30 in) for restaurant seating, enough for a chair to be pushed back. Source: Time-Saver Standards for Building Types (Restaurants); Panero & Zelnik.

q: Under the Water Code, what easement along riverbanks, lakes and seashores applies in agricultural areas, where no structures may be built?
n: The Water Code easement along banks of rivers, lakes and seashores is 3 m in urban areas, 20 m in agricultural areas and 40 m in forest areas. No structures may be built within it. Source: PD 1067 (Water Code), Art. 51.

q: Whattree gives good shade but should be avoided for potential root damage to structures?
n: Acacia (rain tree) gives broad shade, but its wide, shallow roots can lift pavements and damage foundations, so plant it well away from structures. Source: DPWH/NBC landscaping guidelines; arboriculture references.

q: Which terrain is hardest to build on?
n: Very steep terrain is hardest to build on. It needs heavy cut-and-fill, retaining walls and slope protection, and raises erosion and landslide risk. Source: Lynch & Hack, Site Planning.

q: Which shows good site planning?
n: Good site planning maximizes land use, controls environmental hazards and makes maintenance efficient, so all of the choices apply. Source: Lynch & Hack, Site Planning.

q: What happens when severe storms overload urban stormwater systems?
n: When severe storms produce runoff beyond the capacity of urban drainage, the result is surface flooding. Source: DPWH Design Guidelines (Drainage); Lynch & Hack, Site Planning.

q: Which site planning strategies cut energy costs and environmental impact?
o: Minimizing disruption and protecting natural drainage
Responding to climate and reducing water and maintenance
Limiting extension of services and travel
n: Minimizing site disruption, protecting natural drainage, responding to climate and reducing water and energy use all lower energy costs and environmental impact. Source: USGBC LEED / BERDE Green Building Rating System.

q: Which is NOT part of the structural plans?
n: Structural plans include foundation, floor framing and roof framing plans. The site development plan belongs to the architectural set. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule III, Sec. 302.

q: What is the distance from the front (sidewalk) line to the rear of a lot called?
n: Lot depth is the distance from the front (street) line to the rear lot line. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, definitions.

q: As per NSO, what structure is 3 or more units, intended for residential use only, usually consisting of 3 or more housing units?
n: The Philippine Statistics Authority (formerly NSO) census defines a multi-unit residential building as a structure of three or more housing units intended for residential use only. Source: PSA Census of Population and Housing (definitions).

q: Parking areas should be on slopes below what, or else be graded?
n: Parking areas should be on slopes of about 5% or less, or be graded. Steeper surfaces make parked cars roll and hinder access. Source: Time-Saver Standards for Site Planning; Lynch & Hack, Site Planning.

q: What is the open area within the setbacks called?
n: A yard is the open, unoccupied space within the setbacks between the building and the lot lines (front, side, rear). Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VIII.

q: Which street pattern follows the contours of very hilly sites?
n: A curvilinear street pattern follows the contours of hilly sites, limiting grades and earthwork. Source: Lynch & Hack, Site Planning.

q: Which lines show elevations on a topographic map?
n: Contour lines join points of equal elevation and show terrain on a topographic map. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; Lynch & Hack.

q: Inherent site problems include all of these EXCEPT:
n: Abnormal grading, inefficient layout and an awkward street pattern are site problems. Good drainage is an asset, not a problem. Source: Lynch & Hack, Site Planning.

q: Land reserved for transportation use is called a:
n: A right of way is land reserved for transportation use, holding the road, sidewalks and utilities. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, definitions; DPWH.

q: RROW stands for:
n: RROW means road right-of-way, the full legal width of land reserved for a road and its sidewalks. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VIII.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true?
o: A street's three-dimensional form inhibits some activities and enables others
Alberti held that streets in a noble, powerful city should wind rather than be straight and broad
Competition for drivers' attention has made road signs bigger and bolder
A total separation of vehicles and pedestrians is harmful to a lively street
n: Alberti wrote that a noble, powerful city should have straight, broad streets. Winding streets suit smaller towns. So the statement that he wanted winding streets in a noble city is false. Source: Alberti, De re aedificatoria, Book IV.

q: What is a narrow way through a block, often for pedestrians only?
n: An alley is a narrow way through a block, often for pedestrians or service access only. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, definitions; Ching.

q: Which street carries high-speed, high-volume traffic?
n: An arterial street carries high-speed, high-volume through traffic between districts. Collectors feed arterials from local streets. Source: AASHTO Green Book; DPWH road classification.

q: Which road rings an urban area so traffic can bypass the center?
n: A circumferential road rings an urban area so traffic can bypass the center, like Metro Manila's C-1 to C-6. Source: DPWH; MMDA road network.

q: A lot or land intended for construction site can be best described by its__-
n: A construction lot is best described by its Transfer Certificate of Title, which carries its technical description (bearings, distances, area). Source: PD 1529.

q: Which land evaluation method, resting mainly on expert scientific judgment, plans areas that keep key natural features?
n: Land suitability analysis, resting mainly on expert scientific judgment, rates land for proposed uses while keeping key natural features. Source: McHarg, Design with Nature; Steiner, The Living Landscape.

q: Which earthwork method suits linear work like roads, paths and utility trenches?
n: The average end area method suits linear earthwork such as roads, paths and trenches. Volume between stations is the average of the two end cross-section areas times the distance. Source: Davis & Foote, Surveying; Lynch & Hack.

q: Which overlay mapping of natural factors determines a site's suitability for proposed uses?
n: Sieve mapping overlays maps of natural factors (slope, soils, flooding) to screen out unsuitable land and find suitable areas. McHarg popularized it. Source: McHarg, Design with Nature.

q: Site data gathering includes all of these EXCEPT:
o: Land use plans and zoning ordinances
n: Site data gathering includes land use plans and zoning ordinances, base and aerial maps and surveys, and master plans and feasibility studies. None is excluded. Source: Lynch & Hack, Site Planning.

q: Motor courts in subdivisions shall have a right-of-way of no less than ___ meters.
n: Motor courts in subdivisions need a right-of-way of at least 6 m. Source: PD 957 IRR and BP 220 IRR (road hierarchy).

q: What is the required width, in meters, of the major road right-of-way for subdivision projects sized 2.5 hectares or smaller?
n: For subdivision projects of 2.5 ha or less, the major road right-of-way is at least 10 m. Source: PD 957 IRR (Revised 2008), Table on road right-of-way.

q: What is the required width, in meters, of the minor road right-of-way for subdivision projects of 2.5 hectares or smaller?
n: For subdivision projects of 2.5 ha or less, the minor road right-of-way is at least 8 m. Source: PD 957 IRR (Revised 2008).

q: What is the required width, in meters, of the major road right-of-way for subdivision projects between 5 and 10 hectares?
n: For subdivision projects above 5 ha up to 10 ha, the major road right-of-way is at least 12 m. Source: PD 957 IRR (Revised 2008).

q: What is the required width, in meters, of the minor road right-of-way for subdivision projects between 5 and 10 hectares?
n: For subdivision projects above 5 ha up to 10 ha, the minor road right-of-way stays at 8 m. Only the major road widens, to 12 m. Source: PD 957 IRR (Revised 2008), road right-of-way table.

q: Under the PD 957 IRR, what is the minimum frontage of a single-detached corner lot?
n: Under the PD 957 IRR, a single-detached corner lot in an open-market or medium-cost subdivision needs at least 12 m of frontage, because two sides face streets and both setbacks apply. Source: PD 957 IRR (Revised 2008), minimum lot frontage table.
